sections.h2: How Missouri sets the assessed value of a home
sections.html:
Your county assessor lists every parcel each year and applies a fixed share of market value that varies by use. RSMo 137.115 sets houses and other residential land at 19%, farmland at 12% and commercial parcels at 32%. Tangible personal property is taxed on one third of its worth as of January 1.

Missouri revalues land and buildings every other year. The assessor sets fresh figures as of January 1 in odd-numbered years, and those figures stay on the books through the following even year. New construction and added improvements are picked up when completed. The latest reassessment year was 2025, so a 2026 bill rests on that number, and the next general revaluation is 2027. Counties can vote to opt out of the revaluation provisions, so call the assessor's office to confirm your county's schedule.

Residential owners have a safeguard against large jumps. If the assessor wants to raise a home's value more than fifteen percent over the previous one, aside from new construction, an on-site physical inspection must come first, and a look from the street is not enough. You get at least thirty days to ask that the visit include the inside of the house. Anyone whose land is put to a different use may also ask the assessor to reclassify it.

sections.h2: When Missouri property tax is due
sections.html:
Payment goes to the county collector, and the last day is December 31. After that date interest and penalties begin. Collectors can take cards and electronic payments, with any surcharge limited to what the card or payment company charges the county.

If you plan a fall or winter sale, call the collector for the parcel's current balance and ask whether older years are delinquent. Give that number to your closing agent before you agree to terms, so the amount is no surprise at closing.

You do not have to pay before challenging a value, because an appeal is allowed while the bill is still open. The cost of waiting is that unpaid tax keeps accumulating interest and penalties in the meantime.

The first stop is the board that equalizes values in your county, and the filing deadline there is the second Monday in July. A ruling against you can be taken to the State Tax Commission within thirty days of the date on the board's decision letter, using its Complaint for Review of Assessment.

Send the complaint through the Commission's online portal, by email to Legal@stc.mo.gov, or by mail to PO Box 146, Jefferson City, MO 65102-0146. Enclose the tax bill or the board's letter, and hold your other evidence for later in the process. Parcels titled to a corporation, LLC, limited partnership, trust or estate require an attorney to file, or the appeal will be rejected.

An owner may skip the county step and file straight with the Commission in two cases:

  • the assessor never gave the current owner notice of the value, or of an increase, at least thirty days ahead of the county deadline, including when the notice went to a prior owner;
  • the buyer closed within thirty days after the county mailed the tax statement.

Signing an agreed value with the assessor at the county stage ends the dispute for good. In a charter county or the City of St. Louis, a residential value produced by computer puts the burden on the assessor, who must present appraisal findings and three comparable sales.

You pay the whole bill on time while preserving your objection. Send the full amount to the collector before the December 31 cutoff, mark the check "paid under protest", and enclose a written statement of your grounds. When the complaint is about value, the statement has to give the market value you believe is right. A mailing postmarked on or before December 31 counts.

Skipping both steps has a cost. An owner who paid without protest and filed no appeal by the deadline cannot contest that year's assessment. The following year stays open, because an appeal to the equalization board is available again on the same July date.

If you may sell, mark the July date before the house goes on the market. The window is short.

sections.h2: Is there tax relief for older or disabled homeowners?
sections.html:
The Department of Revenue runs a refundable credit known as the circuit breaker. It reimburses a slice of the real estate tax, or rent, that a qualifying senior or a person who is 100 percent disabled paid during the year. Homeowners who lived in their own home can receive up to $1,100, and renters up to $750. The amount you actually get depends on what you paid and on all household income, taxable or not. Tenants of facilities that pay no property tax do not qualify.

Personal property tax questions belong with the county assessor. For the credit, the Department's page offers claim help and the address PropertyTaxCredit@dor.mo.gov. A homeowner thinking about selling can use those contacts to ask how moving would affect a claim.

Delinquent parcels go to the collector's sale on the fourth Monday in August. RSMo 140.150 directs the collector to mail the record owner a first notice, then a certified second notice if the assessed value tops $1,000. An owner who never receives the mail still owes the tax, and payment to the collector is accepted until the moment of sale.

Once a sale happens, RSMo 140.340 lets the owner, a lienholder, an occupant or any other interested party redeem without question during the following year. After that, redemption stays possible, though defeasible, until the purchaser obtains the deed. The price covers the purchase money and sale costs, certificate interest capped at ten percent a year, and any later taxes the purchaser advanced plus eight percent interest on them.

If you owe back taxes and want to sell, ask the collector for a full payoff with interest before August. A sold certificate adds costs to everything that follows. A cash buyer can usually close fast enough to pay the collector from proceeds before that sale date, which a listing with showings and buyer financing may not manage.

faqs.q: What share of a home's value is taxed in Missouri?
faqs.a: Nineteen percent. RSMo 137.115 assesses residential real property at 19% of true value, farmland at 12% and commercial property at 32%.

faqs.q: By what date must a value appeal be filed locally?
faqs.a: The second Monday in July is the filing date at the county equalization board. If the board denies the appeal, the State Tax Commission accepts a complaint within thirty days of the date on the decision letter.

faqs.q: Must the bill be paid first if I plan to appeal?
faqs.a: No. An appeal is allowed while taxes are unpaid. Interest and penalties still build after December 31, so many owners instead pay under protest and file the written statement with the collector.

faqs.q: Is my home revalued each year in Missouri?
faqs.a: Not every year. New values are set in odd-numbered years and stay for the next even year, apart from new construction and improvements. 2025 was the latest general reassessment and 2027 is the next.

faqs.q: Who can claim the Missouri circuit breaker credit?
faqs.a: Certain seniors and people who are 100 percent disabled. The top credit is $1,100 for owner-occupants and $750 for renters, and the exact figure turns on tax or rent paid and total household income.
